more.d: Stone points about 500,000 years old from Kathu Pan, South Africa, carry damage suggesting they tipped hafted spears, the oldest such claim (debated).
On an ancient tidal flat in Sussex, about 480,000 years ago, people butcher horses, rhinos and deer with finely made flint hand-axes; a shin bone is Britain's oldest human fossil.
About 450,000 years ago an ice-dammed lake in the southern North Sea overflows and cuts through the chalk ridge joining England to France (Gupta 2017).
About 430,000 years ago the bodies of about 29 people end up in a deep cave shaft at Atapuerca, Spain; their DNA places them on the Neanderthal line.
Burnt earth, heat-cracked hand-axes and pieces of pyrite at Barnham, Suffolk, about 400,000 years old, are the oldest evidence of people making fire rather than just using it.
more.w: Control of fire by early humans

more.d: About 320,000 years ago people at Olorgesailie, Kenya, make smaller Middle Stone Age tools, bring obsidian from tens of kilometres away and use red pigment.
Skulls from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, dated to about 315,000 years ago, have modern faces but long, low braincases; the oldest fossils assigned to Homo sapiens (debated).

know.d: Fossils from this time vary so much that experts disagree how to name them; Homo heidelbergensis is often used for the ancestors of Neanderthals and modern humans, but the name is debated.
The Acheulean teardrop-shaped hand-axe, first made over 1.7 million years ago, is the standard tool across Africa, Europe and western Asia for more than a million years.
From about 430,000 years ago glacial cycles swing harder, with four large 100,000-year cycles up to the present (the Mid-Brunhes Event).
The largest British ice age reaches the Isles of Scilly and north London and pushes the Thames south into its present valley.
Hearths become common between about 400,000 and 300,000 years ago, at sites such as Beeches Pit in England and Qesem Cave in Israel.
know.w: Control of fire by early humans

papers.t: Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins
papers.why: Oldest human nuclear DNA yet read; shows the 430,000-year-old Sima people were early relatives of Neanderthals.

papers.t: Evidence for Early Hafted Hunting Technology
papers.why: Argues that 500,000-year-old Kathu Pan points were mounted on spears, pushing stone-tipped weapons far back in time.

papers.t: Earliest evidence of making fire
papers.why: Barnham hearths with flint and pyrite show people could strike fire about 400,000 years ago.

papers.t: Two-stage opening of the Dover Strait and the origin of island Britain
papers.why: Sea-floor mapping shows two megafloods (about 450,000 and 160,000 years ago) cut the land bridge to France.

papers.t: Genomic inference of a severe human bottleneck during the Early to Middle Pleistocene transition
papers.why: Infers that human ancestors shrank to about 1,280 breeders between 930,000 and 813,000 years ago (debated).

papers.t: A Pliocene-Pleistocene stack of 57 globally distributed benthic δ18O records
papers.why: The standard 'LR04' curve of global ice volume that defines the marine isotope stages used throughout these eras.

more.t: Homo naledi in Rising Star Cave
more.d: Remains of at least 15 small-brained Homo naledi lie deep in the Rising Star cave system, South Africa, dated to between 335,000 and 236,000 years ago.
Bones of an early Homo sapiens from the Kibish Formation near the Omo River, Ethiopia, at least about 233,000 years old.
A partial skull from Apidima Cave in southern Greece, about 210,000 years old, has been read as the oldest Homo sapiens outside Africa (strongly debated).
Ten wooden throwing spears from a lakeshore at Schöningen, Germany; once dated to 300,000 years or more, re-dated in 2025 to about 200,000 years ago.
An upper jaw from Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, Israel, about 185,000 years old (177,000–194,000), is among the oldest Homo sapiens fossils outside Africa.

Neanderthals break off some 400 stalagmites and arrange them in rings deep inside Bruniquel Cave, France, about 176,500 years ago (uranium-thorium dating), one of the oldest known human constructions.
At Pinnacle Point Cave 13B, South Africa, people eat shellfish and grind ochre about 164,000 years ago, the earliest known regular use of sea foods.
A jaw found by a monk in Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau, at least 160,000 years old, identified as Denisovan from its proteins.
About 160,000 years ago a second outburst flood removes the last of the chalk ridge; from now on Britain is an island whenever sea level is high (Gupta 2017).
A large skull from Harbin in north-east China, at least 146,000 years old, was identified in 2025 as Denisovan from its proteins and mitochondrial DNA, giving the group a face.

know.d: Fossils from Morocco, Ethiopia and South Africa suggest modern humans evolved across the continent rather than in one place (the 'pan-African' view).
know.w: Recent African origin of modern humans

know.d: From roughly 300,000 years ago African toolmakers switch from hand-axes to smaller flakes and points, with pigment use and long-distance exchange.
The Levallois method shapes a stone core so that a flake of planned shape can be struck off; Neanderthals and early modern humans both use it.
A sister group of Neanderthals known mostly from DNA, with fossils from Denisova Cave in Siberia, Xiahe on the Tibetan Plateau and elsewhere in Asia.
Homo sapiens, Neanderthals, Denisovans, Homo naledi and late Homo erectus all live at the same time.

papers.t: New fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco and the pan-African origin of Homo sapiens
papers.why: Pushed the earliest Homo sapiens fossils back to about 315,000 years and to North Africa.

papers.t: Homo naledi, a new species of the genus Homo from the Dinaledi Chamber, South Africa
papers.why: Named a small-brained human species later dated to 335,000–236,000 years ago.

papers.t: The earliest modern humans outside Africa
papers.why: The Misliya jaw shows modern humans in the Levant by about 185,000 years ago.

papers.t: A late Middle Pleistocene Denisovan mandible from the Tibetan Plateau
papers.why: First Denisovan fossil found outside Denisova Cave, identified by ancient proteins.

papers.t: Lower Palaeolithic hunting spears from Germany
papers.why: Announced the Schöningen spears, proof of planned big-game hunting; Hutson et al. 2025 (Science Advances) re-date them to about 200,000 years.

papers.t: Genetic history of an archaic hominin group from Denisova Cave in Siberia
papers.why: Genome from a finger bone revealed the Denisovans and their DNA in present-day Melanesians.

more.d: Eight white-tailed eagle talons with cut marks and polish, about 130,000 years old, from the Neanderthal site at Krapina, Croatia; probably worn as jewellery.

Pieces of a skull and a jaw from a sinkhole near Ramla, Israel, 140,000–120,000 years ago, with over 6,000 stone tools. The finders (Hershkovitz 2021) see a late archaic group that mixed with Neanderthals; others classify the bones as early Neanderthals (debated).
Around 125,000 years ago the climate is at times up to about 2 °C warmer than today and sea level stands about 6–9 m higher.
Stone tools at Jebel Faya in Sharjah, about 125,000 years old, suggest modern humans crossed a greener Arabia (debated who made them).
River gravels beneath Trafalgar Square hold hippopotamus, lion, rhinoceros and straight-tusked elephant bones from the Last Interglacial (about 130,000–115,000 years ago).
Modern humans at Skhul Cave on Mount Carmel bury some of their dead and keep perforated sea shells; dates are uncertain, roughly 120,000–80,000 years ago.
Skullcaps of Solo Man from Ngandong on Java, dated to about 117,000–108,000 years ago, are the last known Homo erectus.

know.d: The Last Interglacial (about 130,000–115,000 years ago) was one of the warmest of the last 800,000 years, with seas 6–9 m higher; a guide to future warming.
Wet phases turn the Sahara and Arabia into savanna with lakes and rivers, opening routes for animals and people out of Africa.
Modern humans reach the Levant and probably Arabia during warm, wet spells, but these early groups leave little trace in people living today.
Neanderthals live from Iberia to the Altai in small, thinly spread groups, hunting big game and making Levallois tools.
Homo erectus, the longest-lived human species (about 2 million years), makes its last known appearance on Java.

papers.t: Evidence for Neandertal Jewelry: Modified White-Tailed Eagle Claws at Krapina
papers.why: Showed cut marks and polish on Krapina eagle talons, Neanderthal ornaments 130,000 years old.

papers.t: The Southern Route “Out of Africa”: Evidence for an Early Expansion of Modern Humans into Arabia
papers.why: Dated the Jebel Faya tools to about 125,000 years and argued for an early route across Arabia.

papers.t: Last appearance of Homo erectus at Ngandong, Java, 117,000–108,000 years ago
papers.why: Settled the age of the Ngandong skulls, the last known Homo erectus.

papers.t: Middle Paleolithic Shell Beads in Israel and Algeria
papers.why: Identified perforated sea shells at Skhul as some of the oldest known beads.

papers.t: Sea-level rise due to polar ice-sheet mass loss during past warm periods
papers.why: Review showing Last Interglacial seas stood 6–9 m above today from shrinking polar ice sheets.

papers.t: Eemian interglacial reconstructed from a Greenland folded ice core
papers.why: Greenland ice core showing the island was about 8 °C warmer in the Eemian, yet its ice sheet survived.

more.d: About 100,000 years ago people at Blombos Cave, South Africa, grind ochre and mix it with bone and charcoal in abalone shells, the oldest known paint kit.
At Qafzeh near Nazareth modern humans bury their dead about 90,000–100,000 years ago; a teenager (Qafzeh 11) lies with red deer antlers in the hands.
Barbed bone harpoon points from Katanda on the Semliki River (DR Congo), about 90,000 years old, used to spear large catfish (date once doubted).
A Neanderthal woman in her mid-40s or older is laid in a hand-dug gully in Shanidar Cave, Iraq, about 75,000 years ago.
About 74,000 years ago Toba in Sumatra produces the largest eruption of the Quaternary, dropping about 5 cm of ash over India; its effect on people is debated.
Red ochre crayon lines on a stone flake from Blombos Cave, about 73,000 years old, the oldest known drawing.
A hand stencil in Liang Metanduno on Muna Island, Sulawesi, at least 67,800 years old, is the oldest known cave art (Oktaviana 2026).
Ostrich-eggshell water containers engraved with hatched patterns, about 60,000 years old, from Diepkloof Rock Shelter, South Africa.

know.d: Beads, engraving, pigments and composite tools appear in Africa long before Europe's Upper Paleolithic, so 'modern' behaviour built up gradually.
From about 115,000 years ago ice sheets grow in steps until the Last Glacial Maximum about 20,000 years ago.
The Toba supereruption was once blamed for a near-extinction of humans; later work in India and Africa finds little sign of a catastrophe.
Homo floresiensis on Flores (about 1.1 m tall) and Homo luzonensis on Luzon show that small human species lived on islands.
Hand stencils in Indonesia show that cave painting began far from Europe and tens of thousands of years earlier than once believed.

papers.t: Emergence of Modern Human Behavior: Middle Stone Age Engravings from South Africa
papers.why: Engraved ochre from Blombos Cave made the case for early symbolic thought in Africa.

papers.t: An abstract drawing from the 73,000-year-old levels at Blombos Cave, South Africa
papers.why: Reported the oldest known drawing, made with an ochre crayon.

papers.t: A new small-bodied hominin from the Late Pleistocene of Flores, Indonesia
papers.why: Described Homo floresiensis, the 'hobbit' of Liang Bua.

papers.t: Middle Paleolithic Assemblages from the Indian Subcontinent Before and After the Toba Super-Eruption
papers.why: Similar stone tools below and above the Toba ash in India argue against a human catastrophe.

papers.t: Rock art from at least 67,800 years ago in Sulawesi
papers.why: Dated a hand stencil on Muna Island as the oldest known cave art.

papers.t: A Late Pleistocene sea level stack
papers.why: Combined sea-level curve for the last 800,000 years, used for coastlines as ice grows.

more.d: Artefacts at Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land are dated to about 65,000 years ago, which would be the earliest human presence in Australia (debated; at least 50,000).

more.t: Grotte Mandrin: early sapiens in France
more.d: A child's tooth and small points show modern humans at Grotte Mandrin in the Rhône valley about 54,000 years ago, between Neanderthal occupations.
DNA from 11 Neanderthals in Chagyrskaya Cave, Altai, about 54,000 years old, includes a father and his teenage daughter (Skov 2022).
Human-like figures and a pig painted in Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi, are at least 51,200 years old, the oldest known figurative scene.
Diprotodon, the marsupial lion and other giant animals disappear across Australia about 46,000 years ago; humans, climate or both are blamed (debated).

more.t: Bacho Kiro: early sapiens in Europe
more.d: Human remains about 46,000 years old from Bacho Kiro Cave, Bulgaria, are among the earliest Homo sapiens in Europe; later individuals had recent Neanderthal ancestors.
A thigh bone from the Irtysh River in western Siberia, about 45,000 years old, gave one of the oldest modern-human genomes.

know.t: The lasting move out of Africa
know.d: Nearly all people outside Africa descend from a dispersal about 70,000–50,000 years ago that spread along southern Asia to Australia.
Non-Africans carry about 1–4% Neanderthal DNA and Melanesians about 4–6% Denisovan DNA from interbreeding on the way.
know.w: Interbreeding between archaic and modern humans

know.t: Sahul and the first sea voyages
know.d: Low seas join Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania into Sahul; reaching it needed several open-sea crossings from Asia.
Big animals disappear first in Australia and later on other continents, at roughly the times people arrive; how much humans caused it is debated.
Greenland ice shows repeated abrupt warmings within decades, followed by slower cooling, through the Last Glacial Period.

papers.t: Human occupation of northern Australia by 65,000 years ago
papers.why: Pushed the arrival of people in Australia back to about 65,000 years (debated).

papers.t: Modern human incursion into Neanderthal territories 54,000 years ago at Mandrin, France
papers.why: A tooth and tools show Homo sapiens in France about 54,000 years ago, between Neanderthal layers.

papers.t: Narrative cave art in Indonesia by 51,200 years ago
papers.why: Dated the Leang Karampuang pig-and-humans scene, the oldest known figurative art.

papers.t: Genetic insights into the social organization of Neanderthals
papers.why: Chagyrskaya genomes reveal small Neanderthal groups with a father and daughter and women moving between groups.

papers.t: Neanderthal ancestry through time: Insights from genomes of ancient and present-day humans
papers.why: Dates the main Neanderthal interbreeding to about 50,500–43,500 years ago.

papers.t: New Ages for the Last Australian Megafauna: Continent-Wide Extinction About 46,000 Years Ago
papers.why: Dating of 28 sites places the loss of Australia's giant animals about 46,000 years ago.
